analysis.one_liner: Sets national caps on power plant sulfur, nitrogen, and mercury pollution using emissions trading, while easing plant permitting rules.
analysis.headline: The bill got three subcommittee hearings in 2003 but never a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set nationwide ceilings on sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury from fossil-fuel power plants, allocating emission allowances to plant owners largely for free and letting them buy and sell the right to pollute. It would also have exempted power plants covered by the trading programs from a core Clean Air Act requirement — the preconstruction review that forces old plants to install modern pollution controls when they are upgraded or expanded [S2]. Supporters, including the Bush administration, which requested the bill, called it a simpler, more predictable system; critics said it would allow more pollution, later, than the existing law already required [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal- and fossil-fuel-fired power plants. They would receive sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury allowances without cost [S3], gain a single national trading program in place of facility-by-facility pollution limits [S2], and be exempted from major-source preconstruction review — the process that otherwise requires plants to upgrade pollution controls when they make major changes [S2, S3]. The bill also bars courts from reviewing how allowances are calculated [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Replaces facility-specific pollution control obligations for power plants with national cap-and-trade programs for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury, with allowances allocated to plant owners without cost [S2, S3].

Exempts units subject to the trading programs, or with specified particulate controls, from being treated as major emitting facilities for preconstruction review and nonattainment plan purposes, removing a trigger that otherwise forces pollution-control upgrades at modified plants [S2].
States that allowance allocation calculations and the values used in them 'shall not be subject to judicial review,' insulating the distribution of allowances from legal challenge [S3].
Stretches compliance far into the future: it directs a study, with peer review through 2009, of whether the 2018 emission limits should be adjusted at all [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People living downwind of power plants, who would breathe more sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and fine particles for longer than under the Clean Air Act's existing plant-by-plant rules, and communities exposed to mercury deposited in lakes and fish. The public also forgoes the health benefits that critics said deeper, faster cuts would have delivered; the cost of the avoided pollution controls is borne as public health damage rather than as a price at the meter.

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces enforceable plant-by-plant limits with a national trading cap, so a plant that buys cheap allowances can keep polluting at full rate while its reductions happen somewhere else; health studies associate exactly this kind of localized exposure with asthma and premature death [S3].

It strips the preconstruction-review trigger (commonly called New Source Review) from plants in the trading programs, removing the main lever that forces aging coal plants to install modern controls when they rebuild or expand [S2, S3].
The caps and free allowances are set in statute, and the allocation math is expressly shielded from judicial review, so if the caps prove too loose the only fix is new legislation [S3].

The strongest good-faith case for it: a single national trading cap gives utilities a clear, cost-effective target and avoids litigation over individual plant upgrades — but that efficiency comes at the price of slower and shallower reductions than the existing law was already producing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have locked in real cuts in some pollutants, but on a slower timeline and at a lower level than the Clean Air Act's existing tools were already delivering, and it gave away the government's strongest enforcement lever over old coal plants in exchange for a trading cap. Even its own structure — free allowances, no judicial review of allocations, a 2018 limit subject to later study — shows the design weighted operator flexibility over health protection. Weighing it honestly: modest guaranteed reductions, purchased at the cost of weakening the rules that were working.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's environment committee took testimony in three subcommittee hearings but the full committee never voted the bill out, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on February 27, 2003 by Senator Inhofe, who took the bill in on behalf of the administration ('by request'), and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works [S3, S5].
The Environment and Public Works Subcommittee on Clean Air, Climate Change, and Nuclear Safety held hearings on April 8 and May 8, 2003, and concluded hearings on June 5, 2003 [S5].
The full committee never marked up or reported the bill, the Senate never voted on it, and the measure died at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Downwind communities and public health kept the existing Clean Air Act tools — including preconstruction review — that the bill would have weakened. Power plant operators avoided the new trading obligations, but did not get the exemptions and free allowances they sought, and spent years in litigation over the rules instead.

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on behalf of the administration and referred it to his own committee; never scheduled a committee vote on it.

for.name: Bush administration
for.what_they_did: Requested the legislation ('by request' on the introduced text) as its Clear Skies initiative.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Held only subcommittee hearings and never voted the bill out; no floor vote ever occurred.

against.name: Democratic and independent members of the Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Minority members of the committee of jurisdiction
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill in committee in favor of stronger competing clean air legislation, leaving it short of the support needed for a markup.

against.name: Environmental and public health groups and Northeastern state attorneys general
against.what_they_did: Argued publicly that the bill would allow more pollution than existing law and pressed for stronger alternatives.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the bill had two Republican sponsors, and contemporaneous reporting described its committee opposition as coming from Democrats and one independent.

industries.note: The bill would have given plant owners free emission allowances for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury, replaced plant-by-plant limits with a national trading cap, and exempted covered plants from preconstruction review that otherwise forces upgrades [S2, S3]. Those concessions are worth billions in avoided pollution-control spending, paid for as public health damage downwind.

A friendlier regulatory path for coal-fired generation, including clean-coal demonstration incentives, would have sustained coal demand longer; but the industry also gained nothing because the bill never passed [S3].
